claims.overstatement: None. The factor is given for cannabinoids in general (THC and its metabolites in the cited reference), not THC alone. 'Has to be multiplied' is a little firmer than the source, which gives 1.6 as the factor to convert whole-blood values to plasma concentrations, but the meaning is the same, and 'second-hand' is correct.
claims.note: Leikin & Watson part only. The 1.6 factor is relayed from refs 34-35: Giroud et al. 2001, plasma or serum to whole-blood ratios of THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH in samples from living and dead people; and Williams & Leikin 1999. Table 2 also lists tetrahydrocannabinol among the drugs whose post-mortem level may change, without a ratio, which fits the claim's point that THC levels after death are hard to read.

anchors.extracted: Whole blood is the usual matrix for quantitation at autopsy and serum the usual clinical matrix. This gives a 12-18% difference for ethanol and, for cannabinoids, a factor of 1.6 to convert whole-blood values to plasma concentrations (refs 34-35, second-hand). Blood drawn later after death also changes in make-up (clotting, fluid shifts).
Tetrahydrocannabinol is listed among drugs in which post-mortem transformation or redistribution may occur, with no heart-to-peripheral ratio given.

claims.overstatement: None. 'Practitioners' review' fits: a narrative review by a clinical toxicologist and a poison-centre pharmacist, presented at a symposium, with no stated methods. The nine questions are relayed as the authors' checklist, not as evidence.
claims.note: Leikin & Watson part only. The nine issues are listed in full on p. 52; the four named in the claim (sampling site, post-mortem change, tolerance, autopsy findings) are items 1, 2, 4 and 6.

anchors.locator: Left column, 2nd paragraph, items 1-2; right column, items 3-9
anchors.extracted: Issues a clinical toxicologist must address to judge a drug's role in a death from quantitative results: (1) multiple sampling sites and where they were; (2) whether the drug is known or suspected to redistribute (Table 2); (3) whether data define the concentration-toxicity relationship; (4) clinical information on the exposure, e.g. tolerance and dosing interval; (5) whether the concentration was clinically sufficient to cause, prevent or be directly involved in the death; (6) characteristic autopsy findings (Table 7); (7) embalming (Table 8); (8) special storage needs (Table 9); (9) whether gastric pills are active drug or a drug-free 'ghost pill'.

anchors.locator: p. 47, 1st paragraph (both columns); p. 48, left column, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Comparing post-mortem levels with ranges from living patients assumed the level does not change during and after death, which the authors call incorrect for many substances. Concentration-effect relationships depend on dose, timing, route, tolerance and steady state, and most come from therapeutic trough levels at steady state.

anchors.locator: Conclusion (p. 52 right column, continuing p. 53 left and right columns)
anchors.extracted: A post-mortem result cannot always be extrapolated to the state before death. Limited knowledge of post-mortem changes can lead to incorrect assumptions, and stability and redistribution must be built into interpretation. Multiple-site sampling and timely ante- and post-mortem assays are needed.

claims.overstatement: Two details overstate or misdescribe the table. (1) 'Ratios for about 100 drugs': Table 2 lists 99 entries (98 substances; venlafaxine appears twice) but gives a ratio for only 82. Two of those are ranges (cocaine 1.5-2.3, imipramine 1.8-2.2), and 16 have no ratio, including THC, pentobarbital, lidocaine, quetiapine and four fentanyl analogues. Suggested wording: 'lists about 100 drugs, with single approximate heart-to-peripheral ratios for about 80'. (2) 'Without case numbers or sources': there are no case numbers and no per-drug sources, but the text attaches the list to 16 references (14, 15, 20-33). 'Without case numbers or per-drug sources' is exact. The table title says redistribution 'may occur'. 'Higher than the compilation's paired medians for several of the same drugs' understates: it is most of them (see note).
claims.note: Leikin & Watson part only. The four example ratios are confirmed on p. 49: morphine (heroin) 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4 (D-methamphetamine listed separately at 2.1), MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5 to 2.3. Editors' comparison with Ketola & Kriikku Table 3 'other blood' paired medians, for the 24 drugs with values in both: Leikin is more than 10% higher for 17 (e.g. morphine 2.2 vs 1.26, methamphetamine 2.4 vs 1.50, oxycodone 3.1 vs 1.19, doxepin 5.5 vs 1.61, amphetamine 2.0 vs 1.43, codeine 1.8 vs 1.16, diazepam 1.6 vs 0.95). Leikin is lower for 3 (chloroquine 3.0 vs 14.61, clozapine 2.8 vs 6.92, fluoxetine 2.9 vs 3.56) and within 10% for 4 (metoprolol, oxazepam, promethazine, venlafaxine). MDMA and cocaine are not in the compilation. Caveat: Ketola's 'other blood' is not only heart blood, and Leikin's peripheral blood is not necessarily femoral.

anchors.locator: Table 2; p. 48 right column, 3rd paragraph; p. 49-50 sentence citing refs 14, 15, 20-33
anchors.extracted: Partial list of drugs in which post-mortem transformation or redistribution may occur, with an approximate heart:peripheral blood ratio: 99 entries (98 substances), ratio for 82, none for 16 (incl. THC, pentobarbital, lidocaine, quetiapine, alfentanil, sufentanil). Morphine (heroin) 2.2, methamphetamine 2.4, D-methamphetamine 2.1, MDMA 2.65, cocaine 1.5-2.3, amphetamine 2.0, codeine 1.8, oxycodone 3.1, doxepin 5.5. No case numbers, no per-drug sources, no ranges of observations. High ratios are taken as greater potential to redistribute, and heart or pericardial samples may read significantly higher than peripheral ones.

anchors.locator: Left column, last paragraph, continuing in right column, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Second-hand (refs 4-7): thiopental and pentobarbital rose significantly in the first 4 h after death; morphine rose significantly within the first minutes against ante- or perimortem samples, but no increase was seen when the first sample was taken 3 h or more after death. A sample at or just before death is needed to show redistribution.

Post-mortem change depends on drug chemistry, tissue breakdown, fluid shifts, pH, volume of distribution and the condition of the body. In supine bodies basic drugs diffuse from the lungs into the left heart, and myocardial release is debated. Table 1 lists about 20 substances in which redistribution probably does not occur (e.g. carbamazepine, hydroxyzine, lamotrigine, mirtazapine, zopiclone, lorazepam, phenobarbital).

Whole blood at autopsy against serum or plasma in the clinic: ethanol differs by 12-18% and cannabinoids by a factor of 1.6 (refs 34-35). The authors' rule of thumb is that drugs with a volume of distribution above 3 L/kg are suggested to be candidates for redistribution. That rule is not borne out by the 2019 compilation, which found no correlation with volume of distribution.

claims.overstatement: None. The source says 'cases' and gives no denominator, study, or what was measured in blood; 'second-hand' and 'a review table reports' describe it correctly.
claims.note: Leikin & Watson part only. The 46% figure is in footnote a to Table 3 with no citation of its own. The text cites refs 41-47 for Table 3, and ref 41 is Jenkins & Lavins 1998 on 6-acetylmorphine detection in post-mortem cerebrospinal fluid, the probable source. The same footnote relays a cerebellum-to-blood morphine ratio of about 1 when death occurs within 1 h and 3.5 when it occurs 2-48 h after administration, relevant to the claim's point on delayed deaths. Table 9 notes that 6-MAM is stable at -20 °C while morphine and its metabolites degrade at 4 °C, so storage can also cause heroin to be missed.

anchors.locator: Table 3, entry Heroin (brain/cerebellum) and footnote a
anchors.extracted: Second-hand: analysing 6-acetylmorphine in cerebrospinal fluid can detect 46% more heroin-related cases than blood. Cerebellum/blood morphine ratio about 1 when death occurs within 1 h, 3.5 when within 2-48 h of administration. Table 3 cites refs 41-47 in the text.

anchors.locator: p. 50 right column, 1st paragraph; p. 53 Table 9, items 8 and 21
anchors.extracted: Vitreous humour can aid quantitative analysis of 6-acetylmorphine (refs 33, 41, 54, 55). Storage: 6-acetylmorphine is stable at -20 °C; morphine and its metabolites degrade at 4 °C but not at -20 °C.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high. I count 5 of 90 references by the authors (refs 4, 9, 27, 35, 83).

interpretation_gap.note: I agree it is 'minor'. The conclusion is cautious, and the over-certain points (Table 1 wording, Table 5 single levels, uncited rules of thumb) are correctly identified. The olanzapine cross-check (0.160 against the Finnish all-cause femoral median of 0.2 mg/L in Ketola & Kriikku Table 1) is confirmed.

missed: Nitrazepam is in Table 1 ('redistribution probably does not occur', p. 48) and also in Table 2 ('transformation or redistribution may occur', no ratio, p. 49). This is consistent only if the Table 2 entry means transformation after death (nitrobenzodiazepines, p. 50), which the table does not say. Minor.

Table 3 footnote a (the 46% figure for 6-acetylmorphine in cerebrospinal fluid) has no citation of its own. The text cites refs 41-47 for Table 3, and ref 41 (Jenkins & Lavins 1998, 6-acetylmorphine detection in post-mortem cerebrospinal fluid) is the probable source. This is worth recording because cl_opi_deaths_heroin_alone relays the figure second-hand.
